To postpone something means to move it to a later time than originally planned.

Think of it this way: you had a plan — a meeting at 3 PM today, a trip next Monday, an exam this Friday. Something comes up, or you make a decision, and now that event is going to happen later than you first intended. That act of pushing it forward in time is called postponing.

The single most important thing to understand about "postpone" is this: the event still happens — it just happens later. You are not canceling it. You are not abandoning it. You are buying more time before it takes place.
Postpone vs. Words That Look Similar

Because several words seem close in meaning, understanding how "postpone" differs from them is essential.

Postpone vs. Cancel
This is the biggest distinction. To cancel something means it will not happen at all — it is called off entirely. To postpone something means it will still happen, just at a different, later time. If a concert is cancelled, you will never see that show. If it is postponed, it has been moved to another date — the show will happen, just not today.

Postpone vs. Delay
These two words are very close in meaning and are often used interchangeably. The subtle difference is that "delay" can be unintentional — traffic can delay you, a storm can delay a flight. "Postpone," on the other hand, almost always describes a deliberate, conscious decision made by a person. You choose to postpone something. Also, "postpone" is slightly more formal than "delay."

Postpone vs. Put off
"Put off" is the everyday, informal way of saying the exact same thing as "postpone." If you say "I'll put off the dentist appointment," you mean the same thing as "I will postpone the dentist appointment." In casual speech, people lean toward "put off"; in formal or professional writing, "postpone" is preferred.

Postpone vs. Defer
"Defer" is also very similar and leans even more formal than "postpone." It is common in legal, financial, and official settings (e.g., "defer a payment," "defer a decision to a committee"). "Defer" can also carry the sense of handing responsibility over to someone else or waiting for a specific condition to be met. "Postpone" is more straightforwardly about moving something to a later time.

Postpone vs. Reschedule
When you reschedule something, you typically assign a new, specific date or time right away — you actively set a new appointment. When you postpone something, you may or may not know the new time yet. You might postpone a meeting to next week and already know the new slot, or you might postpone it without any specific new time in mind yet.
How It Is Used in Sentences

"Postpone" is a transitive verb, which means it needs an object — something that is being postponed.

Basic form:

  • We postponed the meeting.
  • She postponed her trip.
  • The government postponed the election.

With "until" to name the new time:

  • They postponed the match until Saturday.
  • He postponed the surgery until next month.
  • The conference was postponed until further notice.

With "by" to show how much time was added:

  • The launch was postponed by two weeks.
  • She postponed the deadline by three days.

With a gerund (verb + -ing) as the object:

  • He postponed making a decision.
  • They postponed announcing the results.

In the passive voice (very common, especially for official announcements):

  • The game has been postponed due to heavy rain.
  • The exam was postponed because of technical issues.

In the passive form, you focus on the event that was pushed back, without necessarily saying who made the decision. This is why you frequently see it written this way in news headlines and official statements.

In real life, "postpone" is used with a wide range of events and actions:

  • meetings, appointments, exams, elections, matches, games, concerts, surgeries, trials, summits, launches, decisions, payments, weddings, trips, announcements.

Basically, anything that was planned to happen at a specific time can be postponed.

Sometimes, when something is postponed, no new date is set. In this case, people say it has been "postponed indefinitely." This means: we are not sure when it will happen, and we are not committing to a new time right now. It is not the same as cancelled — officially, the event could still happen someday — but in practice, "postponed indefinitely" often signals that the chances of it happening are uncertain or slim.

"Postpone" is a moderately formal word. You will see it in news articles, official emails, business communication, and formal announcements. In everyday conversation with friends, you are more likely to say "put off" or "push back":

  • "Let's put off the trip." (casual)
  • "The meeting has been postponed." (formal/professional)

Both are grammatically correct and mean the same thing. Choosing between them is simply a matter of context and tone.
A Quick Mental Image to Remember It

Picture a timeline — a straight line moving from left (past) to right (future). You have a dot on that line marking when something is supposed to happen. To postpone means to pick up that dot and slide it further to the right. The dot doesn't disappear. It just moves later.

That's all "postpone" means: slide the event to the right on the timeline, by deliberate choice.
